hypothesis.hypothesis:
Use one restoring divider for all four operations. On a valid EX issue, capture the forwarded operands, their magnitudes, and the quotient/remainder and sign controls. Process five dividend bits per cycle for seven iterations, with three leading zero bits before the 32-bit magnitude. Remove the real combinational division and modulo operators.

Use a fixed divide schedule of one launch, seven iteration cycles, and one result transfer, adding eight EX cycles when the bus is ready. Use the same request, latency, and completion logic under RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS, with the existing per-op substitute captured at launch in that build. This keeps the formal gate exercising the new occupancy and forwarding behavior and leaves two cycles of the ten-cycle liveness window for the ordinary inter-retirement spacing, including a preceding redirect under the wrapper's ready-high buses.

Hold the divide in ID/EX and stop fetch while EX waits for its result. Launch only when the older EX/MEM instruction can advance. While waiting, let older MEM and WB work drain and inject a side-effect-free EX/MEM bubble on each unblocked cycle. Keep the result and issue-time operands stable until EX/MEM accepts the result, then pass the result through the existing ALU-result forwarding and retirement path. implementation_notes:
# Shared iterative divider

`DIV`, `DIVU`, `REM`, and `REMU` share a restoring divider in `alu.sv`. It consumes five bits per cycle for seven cycles. A single 35-bit register starts with the padded dividend magnitude and shifts in quotient bits. The result transfer applies sign correction to the registered quotient or remainder. Divide by zero selects an explicit result. Signed overflow needs no separate detection logic because the magnitude arithmetic yields quotient bits `0x80000000` and a zero remainder.

EX launches only when the divider is idle and the older EX/MEM entry can advance. It captures the forwarded source operands for RVFI at launch. ID/EX retains the instruction and fetch holds while EX waits. EX/MEM receives a bubble on each unblocked wait cycle so MEM and WB can drain. The completed divide advances through the existing ALU-result forwarding and writeback path. A ready-bus divide takes nine EX cycles. The `RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS` build captures the existing per-op substitute at launch and uses the same schedule.

## Local verification

- Verilator lint passed in both the real arithmetic and ALTOPS builds. `alu.sv` includes the guarded core declarations when the alphabetical source glob encounters it first.
- `formal/run_all.sh` passed all 53 single-channel ALTOPS checks, including liveness and all four divide instructions, with zero failures.
- All 82 cocotb cases passed. The divider tests cover fixed latency, response backpressure, reset during iteration, consecutive requests, and reference arithmetic. The pipeline test checks launch behind a stalled load, consecutive dependent divide and remainder, and one accepting-edge store with correct RVFI operands, results, and order.
- Co-simulation passed for selftest and all three random programs with zero-wait and stalled buses. CoreMark completed with all canonical CRCs and the validation message. Real divider arithmetic was checked by the cocotb reference vectors and ISS co-simulation.

## Gowin and CoreMark

Gowin placement options 0, 1, and 2 reached 42.639, 45.881, and 45.881 MHz. The median was **45.881 MHz**, up from 5.442 MHz. The option-0 worst setup path ran from the register file through ID, EX, and the ALU to data memory. Its reported arrival time was **28.747 ns across 18 logic cells**, down from 199.837 ns across 156 cells.

With both standard bus stalls enabled, the start and stop markers were at cycles 15,801 and 4,507,286. The **4,491,485 measured cycles** matched a fresh simulation of the baseline. The two `DIVU` retirements fell outside the measured interval. The first, at PC `0x12b8`, moved from cycle 168 to 176. The measured fitness was **102.15 CoreMark iterations/s**, about 8.43 times the baseline at the same cycle count.
lesson: - 2026-11-20 hyp-20261120-001-r1s0 (regression, +742.82%): Replacing combinational DIV/REM with a shared five-bit-per-cycle restoring divider shortened the EX critical path and raised median Fmax from 5.442 to 45.881 MHz, while CoreMark stayed at 4,491,485 measured cycles under bus stalls with both DIVU instructions paying their extra latency outside the timed region.

title: Move DIV and REM into a clocked radix-4 unit
motivation: The baseline Gowin run reports a 199.837 ns, 156-cell path through forwarding and the EX ALU, with a median Fmax of 5.442 MHz. The ALU contains combinational signed and unsigned division and remainder whose outputs pass through the integer result mux. The divider is the leading candidate for the path depth, so splitting it across clocks could shorten the period for every instruction. A baseline Verilator trace with both bus stalls enabled matched the logged 4,491,485 marker-to-marker cycles and passed UART/CRC validation. It retired 93,960 MUL instructions and zero DIV, DIVU, REM or REMU instructions inside those markers, making the divider a candidate for extra latency with no direct cycle cost in the measured workload.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Move DIV, DIVU, REM and REMU into one blocking, clocked radix-4 divider on the EX result path. Capture the forwarded source values and unsigned magnitudes at issue, then register the divisor thresholds D, 2D and 3D. Keep the result pending until EX/MEM accepts it, then forward the registered result through the normal paths and retire it once on channel 0. implementation_notes:
# Clocked radix-4 divider

`div_unit.sv` handles DIV, DIVU, REM and REMU. It captures forwarded operands,
unsigned magnitudes and mode at issue. The next edge registers D, 2D and 3D.
Six recurrence edges process the 36-bit zero-padded dividend in groups of
three radix-4 digits. Each digit uses three parallel 35-bit subtractions and
selects the highest threshold without a borrow. EX/MEM captures the
sign-corrected quotient or remainder eight cycles after issue when ready.
Divide-by-zero, signed overflow and the ALTOPS formulas use the same schedule.

EX holds fetch and ID/EX and sends invalid, control-cleared bubbles to EX/MEM
while the divider runs. An unaccepted older memory request holds EX/MEM and
delays issue. The divider holds its completed result and original operands
until EX/MEM accepts them. The result uses existing forwarding and channel-0
retirement. The 36-bit register shifts dividend digits out and quotient digits
in, sharing storage. A guarded `core_pkg.sv` include in `core.sv` supports the
requested alphabetical Verilator lint command.

## Local checks

- Verilator lint passed in hardware and ALTOPS configurations.
- `bash formal/run_all.sh` passed 53 of 53 single-channel ALTOPS checks on the
  first run, including liveness. The periodic `formal-deep` suite was outside
  this local run.
- `make test TARGET=bench` passed all six runners. The divider unit tests
  cover exact RV32M results, 512 seeded arithmetic cases and result retention
  under backpressure. The pipeline test checks a load-to-divide dependency,
  dependent consecutive divides, immediate ALU and store consumers, a held
  older store, and exact channel-0 retirement and store acceptance.
- Selftest and the three random trace ELFs matched the Python ISS with
  zero-wait buses and with both stalls enabled. Stalled CoreMark passed UART
  and CRC validation.

title: Predict branches and jumps with a 32-entry partial-tag BTB
motivation:
Fetch always advances to PC+4 today. An aligned taken branch or jump
resolved in EX squashes the one younger fetch opportunity, even for a
loop back edge or return that repeatedly takes the same target. A fetch-PC
lookup supplies a cached target in parallel with instruction memory so a
correct prediction removes the squash cycle. A 32-entry scratch RTL
prototype with seven-bit tags cut canonical CoreMark marker-window
cycles from 4,491,485 to 4,191,341 under both bus stalls (+7.16%
iterations per cycle). Gowin placement options measured 5.077, 5.482,
and 5.482 MHz, for 5.482 MHz median and 13.08 iter/sec (+7.9% versus
12.12). Gowin reported 12,766 LUT4 and 30 LUT-RAM blocks for placement
option 0 and identified the forwarded-operand ALU path as critical.

When ID accepts an instruction, advance the fetch PC to its prediction.
Use the current fetch PC as that instruction's predicted successor in EX.
The two positions hold together on a dmem stall, and an imem stall or
load-use bubble admits no new EX instruction. Compare the full fetch PC
with the valid EX instruction's architectural next PC, including PC+4 for

implementation_notes:
# Bench BTB implementation

The 32-entry direct-mapped BTB uses PC bits `[6:2]` for indexing and `[13:7]` for tags. It keeps each tag and saturating direction counter in a 32×9 RAM with two combinational read ports. A separate 32×18 RAM holds aligned target bits `[19:2]`. Reset clears the valid bits. A fetch accepted on a training edge uses the pre-edge entry.

The fetch PC becomes the predicted successor when ID accepts an instruction. EX checks that PC against the full resolved successor of every valid instruction that advances, including non-controls and trapped misaligned transfers. RVFI receives the same successor. A data stall holds both the fetch PC and ID/EX, and EX recovery takes priority over instruction backpressure when EX can advance.

The integration also separates the EX stall signal from the hazard block's redirect-dependent logic so EX advancement can qualify recovery and training directly. Taken updates require an aligned, in-window target. A trap-free not-taken hit updates only the direction counter, since it has no taken target to cache. The guarded type include supports the requested glob-ordered lint invocation.

Partial-tag aliases spaced 16 KiB apart can cause a recovery bubble even on a non-control. Directed tests exercise that case during instruction backpressure, plus JALR retargeting across a data stall, a trained JALR that traps, BTB address bounds, and counter saturation.

- Selftest and three random programs matched the reference in both bus modes. Canonical CoreMark passed all CRCs with both stalls enabled and had no out-of-bounds accesses.
- CoreMark's start and stop markers landed at cycles 15,185 and 4,206,526. The 4,191,341-cycle window improves iterations per cycle by 7.16% over the stated baseline.

title: Shorten the ID-to-EX register operand path
motivation: The champion runs at 45.918 MHz median. In the reproduced Gowin option-0 report, the register-file BSRAM launches both the 28.171 ns path through the EX multiplier to data memory and the 28.135 ns branch path back to fetch. Giving the multiplier its own registered stages left the branch path limiting the median to 45.700 MHz. Both paths need faster register operand delivery.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Shorten the operand path at the existing ID/EX boundary. Implement the asynchronous two-read register file as inferred Gowin distributed RAM with a synchronous write port. Reset a per-register written bitmap and leave the RAM payload free of reset logic. Return zero for x0 and unwritten words, and give a matching nonzero WB write priority on either read port in the same cycle. This avoids the BSRAM clock-to-output delay on the timed EX paths.

When ID accepts an instruction, compare each raw source address with the nonzero destination tags currently in ID/EX and EX/MEM. Capture those four match bits with the operand payload. In the following cycle those producers are in EX/MEM and MEM/WB. Qualify the registered matches with the actual producer reg_write controls at EX, which reflect traps and bubbles. Use mutually exclusive EX/MEM, MEM/WB and register-file enables to drive parallel masked 32-bit operands. EX/MEM takes priority when both writers match. Preserve the held MEM/WB forwarding controls on a data stall even after retirement valid clears. Clear the match bits on the same bubbles as ID/EX, retain them under the existing holds, and use the divider's captured sources throughout its wait.

In isolated prototypes, distributed RAM alone reached 47.678 MHz and registered matches with one-hot selection alone reached 46.381 MHz. Applying both at the operand boundary yielded 54.409, 56.255 and 56.255 MHz across the three Gowin placement options. Option 0 used 3,136 logic cells, 32 LUT-RAM blocks and four BSRAMs. The combined prototype passed canonical CoreMark CRC validation with both bus stalls enabled and matched the champion's 4,491,485 marker-to-marker cycles. The median implies 125.25 iterations/s, about 22.5% above 102.23. The existing divider recurrence became the longest setup path in options 1 and 2.

The combined prototype passed all 53 single-retire ALTOPS formal checks and all six cocotb runners, including directed cases for reset, forwarding priority and a held load result. Selftest and all three random programs matched the reference ISS with zero-wait and stalled buses.

implementation_notes:
# Shorten the ID-to-EX register operand path

The register file infers Gowin distributed RAM with two asynchronous read ports and one synchronous write port. Reset clears the written bitmap, so unwritten registers read as zero. Each read port ORs mutually exclusive masks for the RAM word and same-cycle WB bypass. The write port excludes x0, and the RAM read enable also excludes x0.

ID/EX captures four raw source-tag matches, two for the current EX destination and two for the current MEM destination. The match bits follow the ID/EX reset, bubble, and hold behavior. EX qualifies them with the producers' `reg_write` controls and selects each operand with mutually exclusive masks. EX/MEM has priority over MEM/WB. MEM/WB forwarding uses the held write control and data after retirement valid clears during a data stall. The divider captures the forwarded values on issue for its recurrence and RVFI source reporting.

The implementation follows the proposed stage boundaries. It also uses parallel masks inside the register file to shorten the WB bypass and RAM read selection. Directed cocotb cases cover warm reset, the first post-reset bypass to both read ports, simultaneous producer matches, and load forwarding to a consumer held behind a stalled store. The stalled-store case checks both RVFI source values, contiguous retirement order, and exactly one accepted write.

# 32-entry fetch BTB

The bench core now reads the BTB in parallel with imem. The table uses `PC[6:2]` as its index and `PC[13:7]` as its tag, with a 32×9 metadata RAM, a 32×18 target RAM, and resettable valid bits. A registered EX training record feeds the update port. Taken updates require word-aligned source and target addresses in the 1 MiB instruction window. Untaken branches update the counter on a valid source tag match.

The PC register records the prediction when ID accepts a fetch. EX compares the current fetch address with both candidate successors in parallel and sends the resolved architectural successor to RVFI. Recovery and training wait for EX to advance, including through dmem backpressure and divider holds. Recovery overrides imem stalls and flushes ID/EX. Imem readiness alone controls the combinational instruction mask. The implementation follows the proposed pipeline and preserves the bench core's single-retire RVFI interface and clocked divider.

The partial tag allows addresses 16 KiB apart to alias. Directed cocotb tests confirmed recovery from aliases on ADD and DIVU under imem backpressure. A separate test exercised a cold JALR, a stale JALR target, the updated prediction, and a misaligned JALR trap while older stores stalled on dmem.

# Separate execute paths and shorten the divider recurrence

## Implementation

- EX/MEM registers the full forwarded `rs1 + immediate` byte address. JALR shares the sum and clears bit 0. The data bus, alignment checks, byte lanes, load extraction, and word-aligned RVFI address use the registered address.
- A single signed 33-by-33 multiply uses operation-specific sign extension and registers its low 64 bits alongside the integer result. - Fetch sends raw instruction data and bus readiness to decode. Redirect and load-use bubbles clear ID/EX validity. An older stalled memory instruction holds ID/EX and EX/MEM. The multiply datapath lives in `ex_stage.sv`, where the product and word enables can share the EX/MEM stall boundary. ID can capture a load-use bubble's payload while clearing its valid bit. The distributed register file and registered forwarding matches remain in use.

# Direction-only direct-transfer prediction

## Implementation

A fetch accepted on the write edge uses the pre-edge state.
- Fetch predecodes JAL and the six legal conditional branches. A shared 30-bit word adder forms the direct target, and a separate incrementer forms `PC+4`. # Bench direct-target fetch

EX forms the direct target and its successor with two parallel 30-bit additions. Four byte comparisons resolve branch equality and order. IF offers the aligned target as soon as the transfer resolves. ID/EX captures both PC pairs and the selection bit, so EX can recover the captured instruction's PC and link value. An older dmem stall holds the PC banks and ID/EX while the direct target remains on imem. JALR redirects the registered PC and flushes the younger fetch.

AUIPC uses the direct-target adder. The EX/MEM result register combines the integer ALU, AUIPC, link, and divider outputs with one-hot enables. MEM/WB captures the selected load or EX word for both forwarding and writeback. A dmem stall clears retirement valid and preserves the word, destination, and forwarding eligibility.

PC pairs use word addresses because all fetched instructions are word-aligned. The two direct-target adders use the same selected PC, with a carry-in of one word for the successor. This keeps the sums parallel and lets formal check their relationship locally across consecutive direct transfers. The initial version used the registered PC+4 as the base for the successor and spent several minutes on individual instruction proofs before that run was stopped. # Shared fetch and execute PC

IF uses a two-word fall-through FIFO with independent head and tail valid bits. Each word carries a B, JAL, or JALR opcode predecode. # Implementation notes

## Pipeline

EX/MEM registers the ADD and SUB words, the shared integer and special result word, the full multiply product, and the effective address. MEM uses the registered producer class to select the result or the extended load into MEM/WB. ALTOPS multiply and divide results use the same lanes and register boundaries.

ID registers each operand's one-hot bypass selection using the youngest eligible EX or MEM destination. EX excludes a misaligned jump's link, and MEM excludes a misaligned load. The load-use interlock waits for the load to reach MEM. ALU B has separate immediate-qualified selects, and branches, stores, multiply, divide, and RVFI keep the forwarded rs2.

Data backpressure holds the selectors, EX/MEM lanes, and MEM/WB payload. MEM/WB clears retirement valid on the stall edge. The divider captures forwarded sources at issue and advances its finished result with the instruction. Direct target fetch and retry remain in IF, and the configured single retirement channel is RVFI channel 0.

## Timing changes

The first result-lane implementation measured a 79.839 MHz Gowin median. To shorten the divider path while preserving its issue-to-result latency, the final design uses a registered reciprocal lookup and multiply for divisor magnitudes below 256. The estimate is either exact or one low. A nine-bit remainder calculation determines the correction. The radix-16 recurrence handles larger divisors. Conditional negation uses lower-bit reductions on the input magnitudes and the result.

ID also predecodes the branch predicate controls, and EX resolves signed ordering in the highest byte term. The ALU shares a right shifter between SRL and SRA. These changes shorten paths from forwarded operands. The divider lookup uses one BSRAM. The final design's longest paths run through branch resolution in placement option 0 and through the ALU into the shared integer and special result lane in options 1 and 2.

implementation_notes:
# Target-word replay

The fetch cursor indexes a 64-entry tagged BTB with two-bit counters and distributed target-word storage. Each entry stores the aligned target and its successor. The four-packet queue stores the bus and replay lanes independently. ID issues from queue storage while IF continues filling free slots during load-use, divide and data-bus stalls.

EX compares the predicted successor with the sequential, direct and JALR candidates. ID registers the shared carry-save terms for the target comparisons. EX/MEM holds the direct and sequential candidates and uses the existing effective address for JALR. The resolved successor drives registered repair, predictor training and RVFI. Training pairs consecutive surviving advances and registers the pair before the table write. FENCE.I clears the BTB valid bits and the younger queue and decode state. Logical fetch PCs outside the instruction window retire synthetic illegal words with their full architectural PCs.

The first formal run found a liveness counterexample. A divide immediately after a cold redirect exceeded the check's ten-cycle retirement interval. EX/MEM now holds the resolver through the flush and first refill edge, then advances independently of imem readiness. This overlaps the front-end refill, preserves forwarding, and lets the divider retain its original execution schedule. A fetch opcode bit excludes memory instructions from stale taken predictions, so holding a resolver cannot repeat a data-memory request.

Local formal status was incomplete at the time limit. The final RTL passed 34 of 53 checks with zero reported failures, including liveness, unique retirement order, and both PC continuity checks.

The branch comparator groups two-bit comparisons and the barrel shifter groups its shift amounts to shorten the Gowin paths. A combinational equivalence proof compared all ALU outputs and result lanes against the original implementation for every input. The multiplier, divider and bypass lanes use the existing implementation.

The pipeline tests cover replay during imem stalls, refill during a held dmem request, counter updates, stale JALR target repair, suppression of wrong-path stores and divider issues, FENCE.I with self-modifying code, and instruction-window and alignment cases. The harness checks full retirement order and PC sequences and continues to assert held dmem request stability.

Verilator lint, all six cocotb runners, and single-channel co-simulation passed. The pipeline runner passed all 32 scenarios. Canonical stalled CoreMark completed 10 iterations in 3,819,059 marker cycles, with all five expected CRCs, the validation message, and no out-of-bounds accesses.

The three Gowin placements reached 93.441, 95.128 and 95.128 MHz. The 95.128 MHz median gives 249.09 CoreMark iterations per second, above the 242.034 acceptance threshold. The option 0 critical path runs from a multiplier result to the registered direct-transfer selector. The other two placements are limited by the existing wide divider.

implementation_notes:
# Bench reciprocal divider

The divider captures the forwarded operands and sign information on issue. One unsigned 34-by-35-bit multiplier is reused for the mantissa–seed product, Newton refinement, scaled dividend and quotient–divisor product. The multiplier takes registered operands for all four products. The synchronous 2,048-entry seed ROM reads from a parallel divisor window in phase 1 so its output is ready for the phase-2 operand load. Bit reductions captured on issue shorten the raw-divisor threshold tests and the ROM address path.

Phase 8 forms signed quotient or remainder candidates and the exact correction flag. EX/MEM registers the candidates and flag, and MEM selects the result into the ordinary MEM/WB bypass. A dependent successor waits one cycle for that bypass. An independent successor advances immediately even when its immediate bits match the destination. MEM forwards the prior divide writeback into those raw RVFI operand fields to preserve the retirement trace. Divide-by-zero, signed overflow, ALTOPS, dmem holds and single-channel retirement use the same completion schedule.

The selected implementation also gives the shifter a separate EX/MEM forwarding lane to shorten the ALU result path. Ordered branches bias the operand sign bits for a shared signed and unsigned comparison.

- Verilator `--lint-only -Wall -Wno-MULTITOP` passed.
- All six pytest runners passed, including every reciprocal ROM index, signed threshold boundaries, held completion, dependent divides, JALR into a divide and stalled writeback forwarding.

An earlier invocation also exposed a Yosys syntax error on an ALTOPS struct literal, which was replaced with explicit field assignments.
- Cosimulation passed exact RVFI comparisons for selftest and the three random trace ELFs in zero-wait and stalled modes. The stalled CoreMark run reported 4,148,413 marker cycles over 10 iterations and all five canonical CRCs.

# Divider setup digit

The divider captures the original forwarded sources, operand magnitudes, operation sign, and divisor band at issue. The reciprocal lane uses a registered 4096-entry lookup and exact quotient correction for magnitudes below 4096. The medium lane resolves a digit from the high 14 dividend bits and then takes six radix-8 steps with a 20-bit trial. The wide lane resolves a digit from the high 20 bits and then takes six radix-4 steps. Both lanes qualify the setup comparisons for overflow, register feedback thresholds alongside the first digit, and keep the remainder below the divisor at each step. The setup digit supplies the high bits of the quotient. Setup uses ordered multiplexers to select the first remainder and stores it separately from the feedback remainder. This was the fastest measured implementation.

ID/EX carries mutually exclusive SUB and DIV/REM capture enables. Completed divides use the EX/MEM subtraction word and its adjacent bypass. The divider retains its original seven clocks between issue and `result_valid`, the result-ready hold, the issue-time RVFI operands, the ALTOPS arithmetic, and the architectural divide-by-zero and signed overflow results. Execute also biases the sign bits before the high-byte branch comparison and combines the high and low halves in parallel to shorten the competing branch path. Divider tests now cover every reciprocal divisor, the requested boundaries, all setup digits, overflowed setup multiples, maximum remainders, signed extremes, fixed latency, and held completion. A pipeline test covers adjacent SUB, medium DIVU, wide REMU, and SUB forwarding with exact RVFI sources.

# Steer fetch early and validate target replay alongside decode

The bench core uses a 32-entry direct-mapped predictor and four fetch slots. A short PC tag, the counter forecast, and the accepted opcode select a registered resume cursor. The next cycle compares the saved full in-window tag and exact source word while ID can decode the bus word. Late rejection leaves the source at the head of the architectural stream and restores PC+4. The rejected response consumes no queue credit.

Each slot stores the bus word, its PC pair, the replay target, and four replay words in flat lanes. A registered issue word mirrors the selected lane, with an acceptance bypass for an empty or repaired queue. The mirror can prepare a first replay word from the early guess because a rejection in that case leaves the queue empty. The exact result controls occupancy, the lane index, and the prediction sent to EX. IMEM can fill any free slot during an ID or EX hold.

The training collector reads ordered EX/MEM-to-WB advances and finishes on the fourth word or at a prefix boundary. The update pipeline registers the tag match and counter result before writing the table. Back-to-back updates to the same row forward the pending training result. Fetch reads sample the pre-edge table state for both lookups. A matching not-taken branch changes direction only.

Registered EX repair clears younger work and squashes divider issue. The resolver remains in EX/MEM through the repair edge and can forward its link to the first corrected instruction through MEM/WB. FENCE.I also clears predictor validity and pending training. An out-of-window logical PC uses a parked bus address and retires a synthetic illegal word with the full PC.

ID compares the encoded BRANCH and JAL halfword displacements against two and qualifies each result with its validated decoder control. Synthetic fetches use the canonical zero word for legality.
